sections.title: Module 1: DBMS Fundamentals, Architecture & Data Independence
sections.description: Core foundations of database systems: File System vs DBMS comparison, DBMS vs RDBMS, 1-Tier/2-Tier/3-Tier architectures, ANSI-SPARC 3-Schema model, and Physical vs Logical Data Independence.

topics.title: File System vs DBMS Comparison
topics.what_is_it: A File System stores unstructured files directly on OS disk drives, whereas a Database Management System (DBMS) is a specialized software layer providing centralized, secure, multi-user, and transactionally safe data storage.
topics.simple_explanation:
Before DBMS existed, software applications wrote raw data directly into text, CSV, or binary files on disk. This led to massive issues: if two users updated a file simultaneously, one update would overwrite the other. If a server crashed mid-write, data became corrupted. If an application wanted to find a single record among millions, it had to parse the entire file line-by-line in code.

A DBMS solves all of these problems by managing data centrally. It provides ACID transactions (preventing partial crashes), concurrent locking (preventing multi-user overwrite corruption), indexing (making searches sub-millisecond), and fine-grained security permissions.
topics.real_world_analogy: Storing data in a raw File System is like managing a bank's customer accounts in paper notebooks stored in an unlocked office drawer. Anyone can alter a page, pages can get torn or lost in a fire, and two clerks updating the same balance will mess up the numbers. A DBMS is like a modern digital bank vault with automated access logs, security guards, atomic lock mechanisms, and automatic backup generators.
why_it_exists: Eliminate data redundancy where duplicate information is duplicated across multiple application files.
Prevent data inconsistency resulting from partial updates across scattered files.
Ensure transactional atomicity so that system crashes during execution leave data in a clean state.
Provide concurrent multi-user access control without data corruption or lost updates.
Enforce strict integrity constraints (e.g. balance cannot be negative) at the database tier.
tech_world: Banking systems (HDFC, Chase) use RDBMS engines like PostgreSQL and Oracle to manage account balances transactionally.
E-commerce backends (Amazon, Flipkart) rely on DBMS lock management to prevent double-booking items in stock.
Applications only use raw file systems for unindexed static media assets like images, videos, and PDF downloads.
key_points: Data Redundancy: File systems duplicate data everywhere; DBMS minimizes redundancy via normalization.
Data Consistency: DBMS enforces ACID properties; file systems require manual app-level error handling.
Concurrent Access: DBMS uses locking (2PL) and MVCC; file systems lock entire files or corrupt file pointers.
Crash Recovery: DBMS uses Write-Ahead Logging (WAL); file systems require manual disk repair utilities.
interview_focus: What problems occur when an enterprise relies on raw file systems instead of a DBMS?
How does a DBMS guarantee crash recovery compared to a file system?
Explain Data Redundancy and Data Inconsistency with a real-world scenario.

interview_questions.question: What happens in a File System vs a DBMS if the server crashes during a bank transfer?
interview_questions.answer: In a File System, if the code debits Account A and crashes before crediting Account B, the money disappears permanently (atomicity failure). In a DBMS, the transaction is logged in the Write-Ahead Log (WAL). Upon reboot, the DBMS recovery engine rolls back uncommitted changes, ensuring Account A is never debited without Account B being credited.

interview_questions.question: Why is concurrent file access unsafe in operating system file systems?
interview_questions.answer: File systems lack row-level or table-level locking mechanisms. If two threads open a file concurrently and write at different offsets, OS file buffers overwrite each other, causing race conditions, corrupted file descriptors, and lost updates.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
+--------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ 
| Feature                  | File System                         | DBMS                                |
+--------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ 
| Data Redundancy          | High (Duplicate data everywhere)    | Controlled & Minimized              |
| Data Consistency         | Low (Inconsistent updates)          | High (Enforced via transactions)    |
| Concurrent Access        | Unsafe (File corruption risks)      | Safe (Concurrency control locks)    |
| Crash Recovery           | Manual / No built-in recovery       | Automatic (WAL & Log Recovery)      |
| Data Independence        | No (App tied to file format)        | Yes (Physical & Logical Abstraction)|
| Security & Access Control| Basic OS file permissions           | Granular RBAC (Row/Column level)    |
+--------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
quickRevisionNotes: DBMS eliminates data redundancy, enforces integrity constraints, supports ACID transactions, and automates crash recovery.
File systems lack transactional atomicity, multi-user concurrency control, and logical data abstraction.

topics.title: DBMS vs RDBMS Deep Dive & Codd's 12 Rules
topics.what_is_it: DBMS is the broad software category for managing databases, whereas RDBMS (Relational DBMS) is a structured subset based on Edgar F. Codd's Relational Model storing data in 2D tables with foreign key constraints.
topics.simple_explanation:
Generic DBMS software can store data in flat files, XML trees, or key-value pairs without enforcing relationships between datasets. In contrast, an RDBMS organizes data strictly into tables consisting of Rows (Tuples) and Columns (Attributes).

In an RDBMS, tables are connected using Foreign Keys, and operations are performed using Declarative SQL (Structured Query Language). Furthermore, RDBMS software strictly enforces Codd's 12 Rules (published by IBM researcher E.F. Codd in 1970) which define what makes a database truly relational.
topics.real_world_analogy: A generic DBMS is like an office filing cabinet where documents are stored in folders; you can store anything inside, but finding relationships between two files requires manual effort. An RDBMS is like an Excel workbook where every sheet is a structured table, and VLOOKUP formulas (foreign keys) strictly connect rows between sheets with validated cell data types.
why_it_exists: Structure data into mathematical relations (tables) with predefined column data types.
Eliminate data anomalies by enforcing relational normalization rules (1NF to BCNF).
Establish referential integrity between entities (e.g., an Order cannot exist without a valid Customer ID).
Provide standardized high-level declarative query language (SQL) for complex joins and aggregations.
tech_world: PostgreSQL and MySQL are open-source RDBMS engines powering millions of web applications worldwide.
Oracle Database and MS SQL Server dominate high-security enterprise enterprise transaction processing (OLTP).
Non-relational engines (MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra) are DBMS but not RDBMS.
key_points: Storage Format: DBMS uses flat files / trees; RDBMS uses 2D Tables (Relations).
Relationships: DBMS has no inherent key relationships; RDBMS uses Foreign Keys.
Codd's Rules: 13 rules (numbered 0 to 12) defining relational capabilities. Rule 1 (Information Rule) states all data must be represented as values in tables.
ACID Compliance: Mandatory in RDBMS; optional in many generic NoSQL DBMS implementations.
interview_focus: Are all RDBMS also DBMS? (Yes, but not vice versa).
Explain Codd's Rule 1 (Information Rule) and Rule 3 (Systematic Treatment of NULLs).
Why do commercial databases like PostgreSQL not achieve 100% adherence to all 12 Codd's rules?

interview_questions.question: What is Codd's Rule 1 (The Information Rule)?
interview_questions.answer: Codd's Rule 1 states that all information in a relational database must be represented explicitly at the logical level in exactly one way — by values stored in table cells (rows and columns). Metadata, system catalogs, and table data are all queried identically using SQL.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
+--------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ 
| Attribute                | DBMS (Generic)                      | RDBMS (Relational)                  |
+--------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+ 
| Storage Structure        | File / Tree / Navigational          | Two-dimensional Tables (Relations)  |
| Relationship Enforcement | Manual / Application level          | Foreign Key Constraints             |
| Data Normalization       | Not mandatory                       | Enforced (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF)       |
| ACID Compliance          | Not guaranteed                      | Strictly Guaranteed                 |
| Codd's 12 Rules          | Does not follow                     | Follows Codd's Rules                |
+--------------------------+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
quickRevisionNotes: All RDBMS are DBMS, but not all DBMS are RDBMS.
RDBMS relies on SQL, tabular relations, primary/foreign keys, and strict ACID transactional guarantees.

topics.title: Database System Architecture (1-Tier, 2-Tier, 3-Tier)
topics.what_is_it: Database System Architecture defines how the client UI, application logic, and database storage engine are physically and logically partitioned across hardware nodes.
topics.simple_explanation:
Database systems are architected in tiers depending on scalability and security requirements:

1. **1-Tier Architecture**: The User Interface, Business Logic, and Database engine all run on the exact same machine (e.g. SQLite embedded in a mobile app, or MS Access on a desktop PC). It is fast for local use but impossible to scale for multiple concurrent users over a network.

2. **2-Tier Architecture (Client-Server)**: The client machine runs the UI and Application Code, which connects directly to a remote Database Server over a network via JDBC/ODBC drivers (e.g., legacy desktop apps connecting to Oracle DB). It has security flaws because database credentials reside on client devices.

3. **3-Tier Architecture**: The modern web standard. The Client (Browser/Mobile App) talks to an Application Web Server (Node.js, Spring Boot, Django), which processes authentication and business logic before querying the Database Server tier. Credentials and SQL queries are completely hidden from the end user.
topics.real_world_analogy: 1-Tier is like cooking and eating in your own personal kitchen. 2-Tier is like walking into a restaurant kitchen and telling the chef directly what to cook. 3-Tier is like sitting at a dining table, giving your order to a Waiter (Application Server), who verifies your order and payment before sending it to the Chef (Database Server).
why_it_exists: Prevent direct database access from untrusted client devices.
Allow horizontal scaling of application servers independently from database servers.
Centralize business logic and connection pooling on dedicated backend nodes.
tech_world: Modern web apps (React + Node.js + PostgreSQL) strictly use 3-Tier architecture.
Mobile apps use 1-Tier (SQLite/Room) for offline local caching, and sync to a 3-Tier backend server when online.
key_points: 1-Tier: Everything on 1 local machine. Simple, zero network latency, non-scalable.
2-Tier: Direct Client -> Database connection. Fast, but exposes DB credentials to client and saturates connections.
3-Tier: Client -> App Server -> Database Server. Secure, scalable, industry standard for web applications.
interview_focus: Why is 2-Tier architecture unsuitable for public web applications?
Where does Connection Pooling sit in a 3-Tier architecture?

interview_questions.question: Why is 3-Tier architecture superior to 2-Tier architecture for web security?
interview_questions.answer: In a 2-Tier setup, database IP addresses and credentials must be embedded in the client software, allowing malicious users to decompile the app and issue arbitrary SQL queries. In a 3-Tier setup, the client only talks to the Application Server API; the Database Server remains isolated inside a private cloud VPC network.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
1-Tier:  [ User Interface + Business Logic + Database Engine ] (All on single machine)

2-Tier:  [ Client (UI + App Logic) ] <--- JDBC/ODBC ---> [ Database Server ]

3-Tier:  [ Client (Browser/App) ] <--- HTTP/REST ---> [ Application Server ] <--- Connection Pool ---> [ Database Server ]
quickRevisionNotes: 3-Tier architecture isolates the database tier behind an application server for security, connection management, and independent scaling.

topics.title: Three-Schema Architecture (ANSI-SPARC) & Data Independence
topics.what_is_it: The ANSI-SPARC Three-Schema Architecture divides database design into External, Conceptual, and Internal levels to achieve Physical and Logical Data Independence.
topics.simple_explanation:
To prevent applications from breaking whenever the underlying database storage changes, the database is split into three abstraction levels:

1. **External Level (View Schema)**: How end users and applications see the data. Different users see customized views (e.g. a Student sees their own grades; a Professor sees class performance).
2. **Conceptual Level (Logical Schema)**: The overall blueprint of all tables, columns, data types, and relationships in the entire database (e.g. Tables: Students, Courses, Enrolments).
3. **Internal Level (Physical Schema)**: How data is actually stored on physical disks (e.g., B+ Tree indexes, page block sizes, sequential vs hashed storage, SSD block paths).

**Data Independence** means modifying a lower schema level does NOT require changing higher schema levels:
- **Physical Data Independence**: Changing disk storage, indexes, or file paths (Internal Level) does NOT break SQL queries or table definitions (Conceptual Level).
- **Logical Data Independence**: Adding a new column or table to the database (Conceptual Level) does NOT break existing application views (External Level).
topics.real_world_analogy: Think of driving a car. You interact with the Steering Wheel and Pedals (External Level). Underneath, the Dashboard display organizes speed and fuel status (Conceptual Level). Deep inside, the engine fuel injectors and transmission gears operate (Internal Level). Upgrading from a gas engine to an electric motor (Internal Level change) doesn't change how you turn the steering wheel (External Level).
why_it_exists: Isolate end-user applications from complex physical storage details.
Allow database administrators (DBAs) to tune performance (indexes, partition tables) without breaking application code.
Provide tailored access views for security and role-based access control.
tech_world: Adding a B+ Tree index on `users(email)` alters the Physical Schema to speed up queries without requiring changes to SQL SELECT statements.
Creating a SQL View (`CREATE VIEW user_public AS SELECT id, name FROM users`) protects applications when underlying table structures are refactored.
key_points: External Schema: Customized views tailored for specific application modules.
Conceptual Schema: Complete logical structure of all tables, keys, and constraints.
Internal Schema: Physical byte layout, indexing algorithms, and disk block pointers.
Physical Data Independence: Hiding physical storage/indexing changes from logical schemas.
Logical Data Independence: Hiding table structural expansion from user views.
interview_focus: Explain the difference between Physical Data Independence and Logical Data Independence.
Which type of Data Independence is harder to achieve and why?

interview_questions.question: Which is harder to achieve: Physical or Logical Data Independence?
interview_questions.answer: Logical Data Independence is much harder to achieve. Changing the physical storage (adding an index or moving files to SSD) is transparently handled by the DBMS. However, altering logical structures (such as splitting a table into two during normalization) requires creating complex views to prevent breaking existing application queries.

quickRevisionNotes: Physical Data Independence decouples logical queries from disk storage mechanisms.
Logical Data Independence shields user views from schema expansion.

sections.title: Module 2: Relational Data Model, Database Keys & Integrity Constraints
sections.description: Relational algebra foundations, domain/entity/referential integrity constraints, primary, candidate, super, foreign, composite, and surrogate key design.

topics.title: Relational Data Model Concepts & Terminology
topics.what_is_it: The Relational Model structures data as a collection of two-dimensional mathematical tables called Relations, where rows represent Tuples and columns represent Attributes.
topics.simple_explanation:
Introduced by E.F. Codd in 1970, the relational model translates real-world entities into tabular relations:
- **Relation**: A 2D table of data.
- **Tuple**: A single row in a table representing a specific entity instance (e.g., User #101).
- **Attribute**: A column in a table representing a property (e.g., `email`, `created_at`).
- **Domain**: The set of permissible atomic values for an attribute (e.g., Age must be an integer between 1 and 120).
- **Degree (Arity)**: The total number of columns in a table.
- **Cardinality**: The total number of rows currently in a table.
topics.real_world_analogy: A Relation is like a student attendance register. Each row (Tuple) is an individual student. Each column (Attribute) is a specific detail like Roll Number or Name. The allowed values for Roll Number (positive integers) form the Domain. If there are 5 columns, the Degree is 5. If 40 students are present, the Cardinality is 40.
why_it_exists: Provide mathematical foundation (set theory and predicate logic) for reliable data retrieval.
Ensure data values are atomic (First Normal Form requirement).
Enable declarative SQL operations without procedural pointers.
tech_world: Relational engines enforce strict attribute domain types (`VARCHAR(255)`, `INT`, `TIMESTAMP`).
High degree tables (>50 columns) are often split into normalized tables to reduce disk block read overhead.
key_points: Relation = Table
Tuple = Row
Attribute = Column
Domain = Set of valid values for a column
Degree = Number of Attributes (columns)
Cardinality = Number of Tuples (rows)
interview_focus: What is the difference between Degree and Cardinality of a relation?
Can Cardinality change dynamically while Degree remains fixed?

interview_questions.question: If a table `Users` has 8 columns and 1,000 rows, what are its Degree and Cardinality?
interview_questions.answer: Degree (number of columns) is 8. Cardinality (number of rows) is 1,000. Degree is static based on table schema, while Cardinality dynamically increases or decreases as rows are inserted or deleted.

quickRevisionNotes: Degree = Count of Columns. Cardinality = Count of Rows.
Attributes must have atomic domain values.

topics.title: Database Integrity Constraints Master Class
topics.what_is_it: Integrity Constraints are rules enforced by the RDBMS engine to ensure that data insertion, updating, and deletion maintain correctness, consistency, and valid business logic.
topics.simple_explanation:
Without integrity constraints, invalid data could easily corrupt a database (e.g., negative balance, duplicate user IDs, or orders pointing to non-existent customers). RDBMS engines enforce 4 primary constraints:

1. **Domain Constraint**: Ensures values in a column conform to its specified data type and range (e.g. `age INT CHECK (age >= 18)`).
2. **Entity Integrity Constraint**: States that NO Primary Key attribute can be `NULL`. Every row must be uniquely identifiable.
3. **Referential Integrity Constraint**: Enforces valid relationships between tables via Foreign Keys. A foreign key value in a child table MUST match an existing primary key in the parent table (or be `NULL`).
4. **Key Constraint**: Enforces uniqueness across candidate keys (e.g. `UNIQUE(email)`).
topics.real_world_analogy: Integrity constraints are like passport control at an airport. Domain constraint checks if your passport format is valid. Entity integrity checks that everyone has a unique passport number (no blank IDs). Referential integrity checks that your visa matches a real registered country in the government database.
why_it_exists: Prevent accidental or malicious insertion of corrupted data.
Shift data validation rules from error-prone application code directly into the database engine.
Guarantee valid referential links across tables during `CASCADE DELETE` or `UPDATE` operations.
tech_world: PostgreSQL enforces Foreign Keys with options like `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `ON DELETE RESTRICT`.
Bypassing constraints in production requires explicit `ALTER TABLE DISABLE TRIGGER` commands, which DBAs strictly restrict.
key_points: Domain Constraint: Restricts allowed cell values (Data Type, CHECK, NOT NULL).
Entity Integrity: Primary Keys must be UNIQUE and NOT NULL.
Referential Integrity: Foreign keys must reference existing Primary Key values in target parent table.
Key Constraint: Columns marked UNIQUE cannot contain duplicate non-null values.
interview_focus: What is Referential Integrity and what happens during ON DELETE CASCADE?
Why can a Primary Key never be NULL, whereas a Unique Key can contain NULLs?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between Primary Key constraint and Unique Key constraint regarding NULLs?
interview_questions.answer: Primary Key strictly enforces UNIQUE + NOT NULL (Entity Integrity), allowing zero NULL values. A Unique Key enforces uniqueness but allows NULL values (SQL standard allows multiple NULLs in a Unique column because NULL represents an unknown value).

quickRevisionNotes: Entity Integrity = Primary Key non-null uniqueness.
Referential Integrity = Valid Foreign Key references.

topics.title: Database Keys Master Class (Super, Candidate, Primary, Foreign, Composite, Surrogate)
topics.what_is_it: Database Keys are single columns or groups of columns used to uniquely identify rows within a table and establish referential relationships between tables.
topics.simple_explanation:
Keys are the foundation of relational database design:

- **Super Key**: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row in a table. (Can contain extra redundant attributes).
- **Candidate Key**: A minimal Super Key with NO redundant attributes. (A table can have multiple Candidate Keys).
- **Primary Key**: The specific Candidate Key chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify rows. (Must be NOT NULL).
- **Alternate Key**: Any Candidate Key that was NOT selected as the Primary Key.
- **Foreign Key**: An attribute in a child table that points to the Primary Key of a parent table to enforce referential integrity.
- **Composite Key**: A key made of two or more attributes combined together (e.g. `(order_id, product_id)` in an order items table).
- **Surrogate Key**: An artificial auto-incrementing integer or UUID generated by the DB (`id SERIAL`), having no business meaning.
topics.real_world_analogy: In a university student database: `{SSN, Name, Phone}` is a Super Key (too many extra attributes). Both `{SSN}` and `{Student_ID}` are Candidate Keys (minimal unique identifiers). The DBA picks `{Student_ID}` as the Primary Key. `{SSN}` becomes the Alternate Key. An auto-generated number `1001` assigned by the computer is a Surrogate Key.
why_it_exists: Uniquely identify individual rows out of millions of database records.
Form the underlying index structure (Clustered Index) for fast sub-millisecond B+ Tree lookups.
Enforce referential integrity between parent and child tables.
tech_world: Modern distributed databases (CockroachDB, Spanner) prefer UUID v4 or Snowflake IDs as Surrogate Primary Keys instead of auto-incrementing integers to prevent ID collision during multi-region writes.
key_points: Super Key: Attribute set capable of uniquely identifying a tuple (contains extra fields).
Candidate Key: Minimal Super Key (no sub-set can uniquely identify tuples).
Primary Key: Selected Candidate Key (Unique + NOT NULL).
Alternate Key: Candidate Keys not chosen as Primary Key.
Foreign Key: Refers to Primary Key of another table.
Surrogate Key: System-generated artificial ID with no domain business logic.
interview_focus: What is the difference between a Super Key and a Candidate Key?
When should you use a Composite Key vs a Surrogate Key?

interview_questions.question: What is the relationship between Super Keys, Candidate Keys, and Primary Keys?
interview_questions.answer: All Candidate Keys are Super Keys, but not all Super Keys are Candidate Keys (only minimal Super Keys qualify). The Primary Key is simply one specific Candidate Key selected by the DBA.

quickRevisionNotes: Candidate Key = Minimal Super Key.
Primary Key = Selected Candidate Key (1 per table).

sections.title: Module 3: Entity-Relationship (ER) & Enhanced ER (EER) Modeling
sections.description: ER diagram constructs, entities, weak entities, attributes, mapping cardinalities, and conversion rules from ER diagrams to relational schemas.

topics.title: ER Model Constructs & Attribute Types
topics.what_is_it: An Entity-Relationship (ER) Model is a high-level conceptual blueprint visualizing database structure using Entities, Attributes, and Relationships.
topics.simple_explanation:
Before creating SQL tables, DBAs design an ER Diagram to model real-world business domains:
- **Entity**: A real-world object or concept (e.g. `Student`, `Course`). Represented by a Rectangle.
- **Weak Entity**: An entity that cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone and depends on a Strong Entity via an Identifying Relationship (e.g., `Dependent` dependent on `Employee`). Represented by a Double Rectangle.
- **Attribute Types**:
  1. *Simple/Atomic*: Cannot be divided further (e.g., `Age`).
  2. *Composite*: Can be divided into sub-parts (e.g., `Full_Name` -> `First_Name`, `Last_Name`).
  3. *Single-Valued*: Holds one value for an entity (e.g., `DOB`).
  4. *Multi-Valued*: Holds multiple values (e.g., `Phone_Numbers`). Represented by a Double Oval.
  5. *Derived*: Computed from other attributes (e.g., `Age` derived from `DOB`). Represented by a Dashed Oval.
  6. *Key Attribute*: Uniquely identifies entity (e.g., `Student_ID`). Underlined text.
topics.real_world_analogy: Building a database without an ER diagram is like building a skyscraper without an architectural blueprint. An Entity is like a Room. Attributes are the room features (length, window count). A Multi-valued attribute is like multiple electrical outlets in one room.
why_it_exists: Provide non-technical business stakeholders and developers a common visual framework.
Systematically map business requirements into relational table schemas without structural flaws.
tech_world: Database modeling tools (Lucidchart, dbdiagram.io, ERwin) generate SQL DDL scripts directly from visual ER diagrams.
key_points: Rectangle: Entity
Double Rectangle: Weak Entity
Oval: Attribute
Double Oval: Multi-Valued Attribute
Dashed Oval: Derived Attribute
Diamond: Relationship Set
interview_focus: How do you identify a Weak Entity in an ER Diagram?
How are Multi-Valued Attributes converted into relational tables?

interview_questions.question: How is a Multi-Valued Attribute converted into relational tables during ER-to-Relational mapping?
interview_questions.answer: A Multi-valued attribute cannot stay in the parent table without violating 1NF. It is extracted into a brand-new separate table containing the parent entity's Primary Key and the attribute value, forming a composite primary key.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
ER Diagram Shapes:
[ Entity ]            --> Rectangle
[[ Weak Entity ]]     --> Double Rectangle
( Attribute )         --> Oval
(( Multi-Valued ))    --> Double Oval
(- Derived -)         --> Dashed Oval
< Relationship >      --> Diamond
quickRevisionNotes: Multi-valued attributes require a new table in 1NF.
Weak entities depend on strong entities for primary keys.

topics.title: Mapping Cardinalities & ER to Relational Schema Conversion Rules
topics.what_is_it: Mapping Cardinalities define the number of entity instances that can be associated with another entity instance (1:1, 1:N, N:M), dictating how many relational tables are needed.
topics.simple_explanation:
Converting an ER diagram to SQL relational tables follows strict rules depending on cardinality and participation:

1. **One-to-One (1:1)**: (e.g., Department has 1 Manager). Can be merged into 1 table or kept as 2 tables by placing Foreign Key in either side (preferably the side with Total Participation).
2. **One-to-Many (1:N)**: (e.g., Department has N Employees). Requires 2 tables. Place Foreign Key on the 'Many' (N) side pointing to the Primary Key of 'One' side.
3. **Many-to-Many (N:M)**: (e.g., Students enroll in N Courses, Course has M Students). Requires **3 tables**: Student table, Course table, and a Junction/Junction Table (`Student_Courses`) containing foreign keys of both tables.
topics.real_world_analogy: Think of marriage (1:1), mothers and children (1:N), and actors and movies (N:M). One actor stars in many movies, and one movie features many actors. You cannot put a single 'Movie' column in the Actor table without violating First Normal Form; you need a separate Cast table connecting Actors and Movies.
why_it_exists: Determine the minimum number of tables required to represent an ER diagram without data redundancy.
Correctly position Foreign Keys to enforce relational integrity.
tech_world: ORMs (Hibernate, Prisma) use 1:N and N:M mapping annotations (`@OneToMany`, `@ManyToMany`) to generate appropriate junction tables automatically.
key_points: 1:1 Relationship: 2 tables (FK on side with total participation).
1:N Relationship: 2 tables (FK placed on the 'N' side).
N:M Relationship: 3 tables (Requires new Junction/Bridge table).
Weak Entity: Always mapped into a table containing Strong Entity Primary Key.
interview_focus: What is the minimum number of tables required for an N:M relationship?
Where do you place the Foreign Key in a 1:N relationship?

interview_questions.question: What is the minimum number of tables needed to convert a Binary N:M relationship into relational tables?
interview_questions.answer: Minimum 3 tables: one for Entity A, one for Entity B, and a third Junction Table containing foreign keys referencing Entity A and Entity B as a composite primary key.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
1:N Mapping (Department 1 --- N Employee):
Table: Department (dept_id PK, dept_name)
Table: Employee   (emp_id PK, emp_name, dept_id FK) <-- FK on 'N' side!

N:M Mapping (Student N --- M Course):
Table: Student (student_id PK)
Table: Course  (course_id PK)
Table: Student_Course (student_id FK, course_id FK, PRIMARY KEY(student_id, course_id))
quickRevisionNotes: N:M cardinality requires a separate junction table.
1:N cardinality places foreign key on the 'Many' side.

sections.title: Module 4: Relational Algebra & Relational Calculus
sections.description: Procedural relational algebra operators (Select, Project, Cartesian Product, Union, Set Difference, Rename) and non-procedural Relational Calculus.

topics.title: Relational Algebra Fundamental Operators
topics.what_is_it: Relational Algebra is a procedural query language that takes one or two relations as input and produces a new relation as output using mathematical operators.
topics.simple_explanation:
SQL query optimizers internally convert SQL queries into Relational Algebra expression trees to evaluate execution plans. Fundamental operators include:

1. **Selection (σ)**: Filters rows matching a predicate condition (equivalent to SQL `WHERE`). Operator: $\sigma_{condition}(R)$.
2. **Projection (π)**: Selects specific columns and automatically eliminates duplicate rows (equivalent to SQL `SELECT DISTINCT`). Operator: $\pi_{col1, col2}(R)$.
3. **Union (∪)**: Combines tuples from two union-compatible relations (same degree and domain types).
4. **Set Difference (-)**: Returns tuples in Relation A that are NOT in Relation B.
5. **Cartesian Product (×)**: Combines every row of Relation A with every row of Relation B (Degree = $D_A + D_B$, Cardinality = $C_A \times C_B$).
6. **Rename (ρ)**: Renames a relation or attribute.
topics.real_world_analogy: Selection (σ) is like filtering a spreadsheet to show only students with Grade 'A'. Projection (π) is like hiding all columns except Name and Email. Cartesian Product (×) is like pairing every shirt in your closet with every pair of pants.
why_it_exists: Provides formal mathematical execution semantics for declarative SQL queries.
Allows Query Optimizers to perform algebraic equivalence transformations (e.g. pushing Selection σ below Join ⋈).
tech_world: PostgreSQL query optimizer parses SQL into a Relational Algebra tree and applies algebraic rewriting rules to reduce I/O.
key_points: σ (Selection): Filters Rows.
π (Projection): Filters Columns (removes duplicates).
× (Cartesian Product): Pairs all rows ($C_1 \times C_2$).
∪ (Union) & - (Difference): Requires Union Compatibility (same column domains).
interview_focus: What is Union Compatibility?
What are the Degree and Cardinality of Cartesian Product R × S?

interview_questions.question: If Relation R has 5 rows and 3 columns, and Relation S has 4 rows and 2 columns, what is the Degree and Cardinality of R × S?
interview_questions.answer: Degree (columns) = 3 + 2 = 5 columns. Cardinality (rows) = 5 × 4 = 20 rows.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Selection (WHERE age > 20):   σ_{age > 20}(Students)
Projection (SELECT name):      π_{name}(Students)
Cartesian Product:            Students × Courses
quickRevisionNotes: Selection σ filters rows; Projection π filters columns.
Cartesian Product degree adds, cardinality multiplies.

topics.title: Relational Algebra Joins & Division Operator (÷)
topics.what_is_it: Derived relational operators combine Cartesian Product with Selection (Joins) or compute 'for all' relational queries (Division ÷).
topics.simple_explanation:
Derived operators simplify complex multi-table queries:

1. **Theta Join ($R \bowtie_θ S$)**: Combines Cartesian Product followed by Selection predicate θ: $\sigma_θ(R \times S)$.
2. **Equi Join**: A Theta Join where predicate θ uses only equality (`=`).
3. **Natural Join ($R \bowtie S$)**: Equi-join on all common attribute names between R and S, automatically dropping duplicate join columns.
4. **Division Operator ($R \div S$)**: Finds tuples in R that are associated with ALL tuples in S. Solves 'FOR ALL' or 'EVERY' queries (e.g. Find students who enrolled in ALL required courses).
topics.real_world_analogy: Natural Join is like matching two puzzle pieces that share identical edge labels. Division Operator (÷) is like checking which job applicant possesses ALL the required skills listed in a job posting.
why_it_exists: Avoid writing massive Cartesian Product + Selection formulas in database query engines.
Express universal quantification ('Find entities matching ALL criteria') elegantly.
tech_world: SQL doesn't have a direct `DIVIDE BY` keyword; Division is implemented in SQL using `NOT EXISTS` or `GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT) = total_count`.
key_points: Natural Join (⋈): Joins on matching column names and removes duplicate columns.
Division (÷): Answers 'Find R that matches ALL S'.
Outer Joins (⟕, ⟖, ⟗): Preserves unmatched tuples by padding with NULLs.
interview_focus: How do you implement the Relational Algebra Division operator in SQL?
What is the difference between Natural Join and Equi Join?

interview_questions.question: How do you translate Division Operator (R ÷ S) into standard SQL?
interview_questions.answer: Division is translated into SQL using double `NOT EXISTS` or by grouping: `SELECT student_id FROM Enrolments GROUP BY student_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM RequiredCourses);`

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Natural Join:  Students ⋈ Enrolments
Division:      Enrolments(student_id, course_id) ÷ Courses(course_id)
               --> Returns student_ids who took EVERY course!
quickRevisionNotes: Division operator answers 'Find items that match ALL targets'.
Natural Join automatically matches identical column names.

sections.title: Module 5: SQL Core Clauses, Aggregates & Clause Execution Order
sections.description: SQL declarative execution sequence (FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT) and Aggregate function mechanics.

topics.title: SQL Essential Clauses & Logical Execution Order
topics.what_is_it: Logical SQL Execution Order is the exact sequential pipeline by which an RDBMS engine evaluates a query, which differs completely from written SQL syntax order.
topics.simple_explanation:
Although you write a SQL query starting with `SELECT`, the database engine processes `SELECT` near the end! Understanding execution order is critical to avoid syntax errors like using column aliases in `WHERE` clauses:

**Logical Execution Order**:
1. **FROM & JOIN**: Identifies target tables and executes join logic to build working dataset.
2. **WHERE**: Filters individual raw rows *before* aggregation.
3. **GROUP BY**: Collapses filtered rows into summary groups based on group keys.
4. **HAVING**: Filters aggregated summary groups *after* `GROUP BY`.
5. **SELECT**: Computes expressions and projects desired columns (Column Aliases created HERE).
6. **DISTINCT**: Removes duplicate rows from projected output.
7. **ORDER BY**: Sorts final result set (Can use Column Aliases because SELECT ran first!).
8. **LIMIT / OFFSET**: Restricts output row count.
topics.real_world_analogy: Think of organizing a marathon. `FROM` gathers all registered runners. `WHERE` filters out runners without bibs. `GROUP BY` groups runners by age category. `HAVING` filters out age groups with under 5 participants. `SELECT` prints certificates. `ORDER BY` ranks fast finishers. `LIMIT` awards medals to top 3.
why_it_exists: Explains why column aliases defined in `SELECT` cannot be used in `WHERE` or `GROUP BY` clauses.
Explains why aggregate functions (`SUM`, `COUNT`) are invalid in `WHERE` clauses but valid in `HAVING` clauses.
tech_world: Query compilers parse SQL into logical tree nodes matching this execution sequence before cost optimization.
key_points: Written Syntax Order: SELECT -> FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.
Logical Execution Order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.
Column Aliases: Created in step 5 (SELECT), so valid ONLY in ORDER BY (step 7).
interview_focus: Why can't you use a SELECT column alias in a WHERE clause?
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING filters?

interview_questions.question: Why does `SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_sal FROM emp WHERE annual_sal > 50000;` fail with an error in SQL?
interview_questions.answer: Because `WHERE` (Step 2) is evaluated BEFORE `SELECT` (Step 5). At the time `WHERE` executes, the alias `annual_sal` does not yet exist. The expression must be written as `WHERE salary * 12 > 50000`.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Logical Order Flow:
[1. FROM / JOIN] --> [2. WHERE] --> [3. GROUP BY] --> [4. HAVING]
--> [5. SELECT] --> [6. DISTINCT] --> [7. ORDER BY] --> [8. LIMIT]
quickRevisionNotes: Execution Order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

topics.title: Aggregate Functions & NULL Behavior
topics.what_is_it: SQL Aggregate Functions (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) compute a single summary value over a set of row values, automatically ignoring NULL values (except `COUNT(*)`).
topics.simple_explanation:
Aggregate functions perform computations over groups of rows:
- **`COUNT(*)`**: Counts ALL rows in a table/group, including rows containing NULLs.
- **`COUNT(column)`**: Counts only rows where `column` is NOT NULL.
- **`SUM(column)` / `AVG(column)`**: Sums or averages non-null values. If all rows are NULL, returns `NULL` (except `COUNT` which returns 0).

**CRITICAL NULL TRAP**: `AVG(salary)` divides the sum by the count of NON-NULL rows! If a table has 4 rows with salaries `[100, 200, NULL, 300]`, `AVG(salary)` evaluates to `600 / 3 = 200` (ignoring NULL row). If you want NULL treated as 0, you must explicitly write `AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0))`, which evaluates to `600 / 4 = 150`!
topics.real_world_analogy: If 3 students score 80, 90, and 1 student was absent (NULL), calculating class test average ignoring absent student yields `170 / 2 = 85`. Giving the absent student zero yields `170 / 3 = 56.6`. Aggregate functions by default ignore absent students unless `COALESCE` is used.
why_it_exists: Provide high-speed summary analytics without transferring raw rows to application memory.
Allow grouping metrics per department, category, or time window.
tech_world: Data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery) heavily optimize aggregate function execution using SIMD vector instructions.
key_points: COUNT(*): Includes NULL rows.
COUNT(col): Excludes NULL rows.
SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX: Ignores NULL values.
COALESCE(val, default): Replaces NULL with fallback default before aggregation.
interview_focus: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name)?
How does NULL affect AVG() calculations in SQL?

interview_questions.question: Given table T with column X containing values `(10, 20, NULL)`, what are the outputs of `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(X)`, and `AVG(X)`?
interview_questions.answer: `COUNT(*)` = 3 (counts all rows). `COUNT(X)` = 2 (ignores NULL). `AVG(X)` = 15 (`(10 + 20) / 2 = 15`).

topics.syntaxOrCode:
SELECT 
    COUNT(*) AS total_rows,                  -- 3
    COUNT(bonus) AS non_null_bonuses,        -- 2
    AVG(bonus) AS avg_ignoring_null,         -- (100 + 200) / 2 = 150
    AVG(COALESCE(bonus, 0)) AS avg_with_zero  -- (100 + 200 + 0) / 3 = 100
FROM Employees;
quickRevisionNotes: COUNT(*) counts all rows; aggregate functions ignore NULLs.
Use COALESCE(col, 0) inside AVG if NULL should count as zero.

sections.title: Module 6: SQL Three-Valued Logic, NULL Handling & Deduplication
sections.description: SQL 3VL mechanics (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN), the NOT IN NULL trap, COALESCE/NULLIF, and row deduplication via CTEs and Window Functions.

topics.title: Three-Valued Logic, NULL Handling & The NOT IN Trap
topics.what_is_it: SQL uses Three-Valued Logic (3VL) where boolean expressions evaluate to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN (represented by NULL). Comparing anything to NULL yields UNKNOWN.
topics.simple_explanation:
In standard math, `x = 5` is either True or False. In SQL, if `x` is `NULL` (unknown), `x = 5` evaluates to `UNKNOWN`! Because `WHERE` clauses only return rows evaluating to `TRUE`, `WHERE col = NULL` returns ZERO rows! You must use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

**THE NOT IN NULL TRAP (MUST KNOW FOR INTERVIEWS)**:
Suppose you query `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)`. SQL expands this to:
`WHERE id <> 1 AND id <> 2 AND id <> NULL`.
Since `id <> NULL` evaluates to `UNKNOWN`, `TRUE AND UNKNOWN` yields `UNKNOWN`! As a result, the entire query returns **ZERO ROWS**, even if `id` is 99! Always use `NOT EXISTS` or filter out NULLs in subqueries!
topics.real_world_analogy: If you ask 'Is John's height equal to 6 feet?' and you don't know John's height (NULL), the answer isn't Yes or No — it is 'Unknown'. If you ask 'Is anyone in the room NOT named Bob?' and there is a masked person whose name is unknown, you cannot guarantee Yes.
why_it_exists: Represent missing, unassigned, or unknown real-world data gracefully.
Enforce strict logical evaluation avoiding false assumptions about missing data.
tech_world: Production outages occur when developers write `WHERE status NOT IN (SELECT status FROM blacklisted_states)` if `blacklisted_states` contains a single NULL value.
key_points: NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN (not TRUE!).
WHERE clause filters out UNKNOWN and FALSE rows.
NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery set ALWAYS returns 0 rows!
Fix: Use `NOT EXISTS` or `WHERE subquery_col IS NOT NULL`.
interview_focus: Why does `WHERE col NOT IN (SELECT x FROM table)` return 0 rows if x contains a NULL?
How do `COALESCE` and `NULLIF` work?

interview_questions.question: Why is `NOT EXISTS` safer than `NOT IN` when dealing with subqueries?
interview_questions.answer: `NOT IN` uses equality operators (`<>`), which evaluate to `UNKNOWN` if any subquery row is `NULL`, causing the outer query to return 0 rows. `NOT EXISTS` checks for row existence via boolean subquery evaluation, making it immune to NULL values in the subquery columns.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
-- THE BUG (Returns 0 rows!):
SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM Branch); -- If manager_id has NULL!

-- THE FIX (Use NOT EXISTS):
SELECT * FROM Customers c 
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Branch b WHERE b.manager_id = c.id
);
quickRevisionNotes: NULL comparisons require IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
NOT IN with NULL subqueries fails completely; use NOT EXISTS.

topics.title: SQL Row Deduplication Techniques
topics.what_is_it: Row Deduplication is the process of identifying and deleting duplicate records from a table while retaining exactly one clean instance.
topics.simple_explanation:
Duplicate data frequently enters production databases due to missing UNIQUE constraints or retry glitches. Deduplication techniques include:

1. **`GROUP BY` with `MIN(id)` / `MAX(id)`**: Works when duplicates can be grouped by business keys, keeping the lowest or highest primary key `id`.
2. **CTEs with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY id)`**: The industry-standard approach. Partitions data by business key (e.g. `email`) and assigns incremental row numbers (1, 2, 3...). Delete rows where `row_num > 1`.
3. **PostgreSQL `USING` Join**: Deletes duplicate rows directly by comparing primary keys in a self-join.
topics.real_world_analogy: Imagine a stack of identical duplicate invoices. Deduplication is like scanning through the stack, stamping 'Original' on the first invoice you find for each invoice number, and throwing all identical copies into the shredder.
why_it_exists: Clean legacy data before applying UNIQUE database constraints.
Prevent inflated aggregate reporting metrics caused by double-counted transactions.
tech_world: ETL data pipelines run deduplication CTE queries in staging tables before loading clean data into analytical data warehouses.
key_points: ROW_NUMBER(): Partitions rows by duplicate keys and assigns unique sequence numbers.
ROW_NUMBER() > 1: Identifies redundant duplicate rows for targeted deletion.
Prevention: Add `UNIQUE` index after deduplicating to prevent re-entry.
interview_focus: Write a SQL query to delete duplicate rows from a table keeping only the latest record.
What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK()?

interview_questions.question: Write a query to delete duplicate email records from a `Users` table keeping the record with the smallest `id`.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
WITH DeduppedCTE AS (
    SELECT 
        id,
        email,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY email 
            ORDER BY created_at DESC
        ) AS row_num
    FROM Users
)
DELETE FROM Users 
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT id FROM DeduppedCTE WHERE row_num > 1
);
quickRevisionNotes: Use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) in a CTE to clean duplicates.
Filter row_num > 1 to target duplicate records for deletion.

sections.title: Module 7: SQL Joins Deep Dive & Join Behavior
sections.description: Comprehensive join mechanics (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, SELF, CROSS) and the critical ON vs WHERE filtering trap in outer joins.

topics.title: SQL Joins Deep Dive (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, SELF, CROSS)
topics.what_is_it: SQL Joins combine columns from one or more tables based on related key columns, matching rows logically via relational set algebra.
topics.simple_explanation:
Joins are used to reconstruct relational data stored across normalized tables:

1. **INNER JOIN**: Returns ONLY rows where join keys match in BOTH left and right tables.
2. **LEFT (OUTER) JOIN**: Returns ALL rows from left table, plus matching rows from right table. Unmatched right side columns are filled with `NULL`.
3. **RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN**: Returns ALL rows from right table, plus matching rows from left table.
4. **FULL (OUTER) JOIN**: Returns ALL rows from both tables. Unmatched columns on either side are filled with `NULL`.
5. **CROSS JOIN**: Produces Cartesian Product ($M \times N$) pairing every left row with every right row.
6. **SELF JOIN**: Joins a table with itself (e.g. Employee table joined with itself to match `employee_id` with `manager_id`).
topics.real_world_analogy: Imagine a list of Students and a list of Hostel Rooms. INNER JOIN lists only students who have an assigned hostel room. LEFT JOIN lists ALL students, showing room numbers for assigned ones and NULL for day scholars. FULL JOIN lists all students and all rooms, including empty unassigned rooms. SELF JOIN is like matching an employee to their supervisor in an org chart.
why_it_exists: Reconstruct normalized data entities across multi-table relationships.
Retrieve combined records in a single declarative query without multiple procedural round-trips.
tech_world: Query engines optimize joins using physical algorithms like Hash Join, Sort-Merge Join, or Index Nested Loop Join.
key_points: INNER JOIN: Set intersection ($A \cap B$).
LEFT JOIN: Left table $A$ + matched $B$.
FULL JOIN: Union ($A \cup B$) with NULL padding.
CROSS JOIN: Cartesian product ($A \times B$).
interview_focus: What is a Self Join and when is it required?
How does SQL handle NULL values during join comparisons?

interview_questions.question: Write a SQL query using a Self Join to find all employees who earn more than their direct manager.
interview_questions.answer:
SELECT e.name AS Employee, e.salary 
FROM Employees e 
JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id 
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

topics.syntaxOrCode:
-- Inner Join:
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name 
FROM Employees e 
INNER JOIN Departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;

-- Self Join:
SELECT e.name AS emp, m.name AS manager 
FROM Employees e 
LEFT JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
quickRevisionNotes: INNER JOIN = Matching rows only.
LEFT JOIN = All left rows + matching right rows.
SELF JOIN = Table joined with itself for hierarchical relationships.

topics.title: ON vs WHERE Filtering Trap in LEFT JOINs
topics.what_is_it: The ON vs WHERE filtering trap occurs when filtering conditions on outer-joined right-side tables are placed in the `WHERE` clause instead of the `ON` clause, inadvertently turning a `LEFT JOIN` into an `INNER JOIN`.
topics.simple_explanation:
Understanding where predicate filters are evaluated in outer joins is a major interview topic:

- **Condition in `ON` Clause**: Evaluated *during* join execution. If a right-table row fails the `ON` condition, the left-table row is STILL preserved in the output with `NULL` for right-table columns.
- **Condition in `WHERE` Clause**: Evaluated *after* the join has generated NULL-padded rows. If the `WHERE` clause checks `WHERE right_table.status = 'ACTIVE'`, the `NULL` value in unmatched left rows fails the condition, dropping unmatched left rows from the result set!

This silently converts your `LEFT JOIN` into a restrictive `INNER JOIN`!
topics.real_world_analogy: Imagine a list of All Customers and their 2026 Purchases. If you put `ON (p.year = 2026)` in the join, customers with no purchases in 2026 still appear on your customer list with NULL purchases. If you put `WHERE p.year = 2026`, customers with no 2026 purchases get filtered out of the list entirely!
why_it_exists: Explains the execution semantics of outer join predicate evaluation.
Prevents reporting bugs where total entity counts drop unexpectedly.
tech_world: Query optimizers optimize `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.col IS NOT NULL` by automatically rewriting it into an `INNER JOIN` to use faster join algorithms.
key_points: ON clause filters right-side rows BEFORE padding left-side unmatched rows with NULL.
WHERE clause filters rows AFTER outer join padding is complete.
Filtering right-table non-null columns in WHERE forces INNER JOIN behavior.
interview_focus: What is the difference in output between placing a right-table condition in the ON clause vs the WHERE clause of a LEFT JOIN?
How do you preserve all left table rows while filtering right table records?

interview_questions.question: What happens to unmatched Left Table rows if you write `LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.cust_id WHERE o.order_date > '2026-01-01'`?
interview_questions.answer: Unmatched left table customers generate NULLs for `o.order_date`. The `WHERE` clause evaluates `NULL > '2026-01-01'` as `UNKNOWN`, filtering out unmatched left customers entirely. This converts the query into an INNER JOIN. To keep unmatched customers, put `AND o.order_date > '2026-01-01'` in the `ON` clause!

topics.syntaxOrCode:
-- PRESERVES ALL CUSTOMERS (Correct Outer Join):
SELECT c.name, o.amount 
FROM Customers c 
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.cust_id AND o.amount > 100;

-- TURNS INTO INNER JOIN (Silently drops customers without orders > 100):
SELECT c.name, o.amount 
FROM Customers c 
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.cust_id 
WHERE o.amount > 100;
quickRevisionNotes: Put right-table filters in the ON clause to keep all left rows.
Putting right-table filters in WHERE converts LEFT JOIN into INNER JOIN.

sections.title: Module 8: Subqueries, Correlated Subqueries & Quantifiers
sections.description: Nested subqueries, correlated execution, EXISTS vs IN performance, and quantifiers (ANY, ALL, UNION vs UNION ALL).

topics.title: Subqueries, EXISTS & Quantifiers (ANY, ALL, UNION)
topics.what_is_it: Subqueries are SQL queries nested inside another query (in `SELECT`, `FROM`, or `WHERE` clauses). Correlated subqueries reference columns from outer query rows.
topics.simple_explanation:
Subqueries allow complex multi-step data evaluation:

1. **Scalar Subquery**: Returns exactly 1 row and 1 column (a single value).
2. **Multi-Row Subquery**: Returns a single column with multiple rows; used with `IN`, `ANY`, `ALL` operators.
3. **Correlated Subquery**: Evaluates once for *every single row* processed by the outer query because it references outer table columns (e.g. Find employees earning more than their specific department's average).
4. **`EXISTS` vs `IN`**: `EXISTS` returns `TRUE` as soon as a matching row is found (short-circuit boolean evaluation). `IN` builds the entire subquery dataset in memory before searching.
5. **`UNION` vs `UNION ALL`**: `UNION` combines result sets and performs an expensive deduplication sort; `UNION ALL` simply concatenates result sets without sorting (much faster!).
topics.real_world_analogy: A non-correlated subquery is like printing a list of high-school pass marks once, then comparing every student against that single printed paper. A Correlated Subquery is like walking to each individual student, calculating that specific student's local classroom average, and comparing the student against their own classroom.
why_it_exists: Perform multi-stage data filtering in a single query.
Express set existential checks (`EXISTS`) and set quantifiers (`ANY`, `ALL`).
tech_world: Always prefer `UNION ALL` over `UNION` in production unless row deduplication is explicitly required by business logic.
key_points: Correlated Subquery: Executed once per outer query row (O(N*M) unless optimized to Semi-Join).
EXISTS: Short-circuits on first match; safe with NULL values.
UNION ALL: Concatenates result sets without sorting (O(1) memory overhead).
UNION: Sorts and deduplicates combined result sets (O(N log N) overhead).
interview_focus: What is a Correlated Subquery and why can it be slow?
What is the performance difference between UNION and UNION ALL?

interview_questions.question: Why is `UNION ALL` faster than `UNION` in SQL execution?
interview_questions.answer: `UNION` forces the database engine to perform a distinct sort operation over the combined dataset to eliminate duplicate rows ($O(N \log N)$ CPU/memory cost). `UNION ALL` appends datasets without checking for duplicates ($O(1)$ overhead).

quickRevisionNotes: Correlated subqueries evaluate for every outer row.
UNION ALL is faster than UNION because it skips deduplication sorting.

sections.title: Module 9: Advanced SQL: CTEs, Recursive CTEs, Window Functions & CASE
sections.description: Common Table Expressions (CTEs), Recursive CTEs for hierarchy traversal, Window Functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, Framing), and CASE expressions.

topics.title: Advanced SQL (CTEs, Recursive CTEs, Window Functions, CASE)
topics.what_is_it: Advanced SQL features allow processing complex analytical data: Common Table Expressions (CTEs) modularize queries, Recursive CTEs traverse hierarchical graphs, and Window Functions compute calculations across row sets without collapsing rows.
topics.simple_explanation:
1. **CTE (`WITH` clause)**: Temporary named result set improving query readability and reusability compared to messy nested subqueries.
2. **Recursive CTE**: Self-referencing CTE used to query hierarchical data trees (e.g. Org charts, bill of materials, category trees).
3. **Window Functions**: Unlike `GROUP BY` (which collapses rows into a single summary row), Window Functions compute aggregate or ranking values over a partition of rows while **preserving every individual row in the output**!
   - Syntax: `FUNCTION() OVER (PARTITION BY col ORDER BY col ROWS BETWEEN ...)`
   - Ranking Functions: `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, `DENSE_RANK()`, `NTILE()`
   - Value Functions: `LAG()` (previous row value), `LEAD()` (next row value), `FIRST_VALUE()`, `LAST_VALUE()`.
topics.real_world_analogy: Group By is like calculating the average score of a high school class and printing a single summary sheet showing only the average `82%`. A Window Function is like handing back every student's individual test paper showing their personal score `88%` alongside the class average `82%` printed next to it.
why_it_exists: Perform complex analytics (Running Totals, Moving Averages, Year-over-Year growth) without multiple expensive self-joins.
Traverse tree/graph structures recursively in a single SQL call.
tech_world: Window functions (`ROW_NUMBER()`, `LAG()`) are mandatory requirements for Data Engineers and Backend Engineers building analytics dashboards.
key_points: Window Functions preserve original row cardinality (no collapsing).
ROW_NUMBER(): Sequential integers (1, 2, 3, 4).
RANK(): Leaves gaps on ties (1, 2, 2, 4).
DENSE_RANK(): No gaps on ties (1, 2, 2, 3).
LAG(col, 1): Accesses data from 1 row prior in the window frame.
interview_focus: What is the difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK()?
How do you calculate a Running Total or Moving Average in SQL?

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() when ties occur?
interview_questions.answer:
For values `[100, 90, 90, 80]`:
- `ROW_NUMBER()` gives `1, 2, 3, 4` (arbitrary tie-breaking).
- `RANK()` gives `1, 2, 2, 4` (leaves gaps after ties).
- `DENSE_RANK()` gives `1, 2, 2, 3` (no gaps after ties).

topics.syntaxOrCode:
-- Top 2 Salaries per Department using Window Function:
WITH RankedSalaries AS (
    SELECT 
        emp_id,
        dept_id,
        salary,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY dept_id 
            ORDER BY salary DESC
        ) as rnk
    FROM Employees
)
SELECT * FROM RankedSalaries WHERE rnk <= 2;

-- Running Total Example:
SELECT 
    trans_date,
    amount,
    SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY trans_date) AS running_total
FROM Transactions;
quickRevisionNotes: Window Functions keep all individual rows while adding computed aggregate columns.
DENSE_RANK() leaves no gaps on ties; RANK() leaves gaps.

sections.title: Module 10: Functional Dependencies, Normalization & Denormalization
sections.description: Database anomalies, Functional Dependencies, Closure sets, Candidate Key finding algorithm, Normal Forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF), and Denormalization.

topics.title: Why Normalize? Database Anomalies & Functional Dependencies
topics.what_is_it: Normalization is the systematic process of organizing database schema to eliminate data redundancy and prevent Insertion, Update, and Deletion Anomalies.
topics.simple_explanation:
Poor database design places unrelated attributes in a single table, causing three severe anomalies:

1. **Insertion Anomaly**: Cannot insert data about an entity without adding data about another unrelated entity (e.g. Cannot add a new Department unless at least one Employee is assigned to it).
2. **Update Anomaly**: Updating a single piece of data (e.g. Department Name) requires updating hundreds of duplicate rows; if one row is missed, data becomes inconsistent.
3. **Deletion Anomaly**: Deleting a row (e.g. deleting the last Employee in a department) accidentally deletes the entire Department record from the database!

**Functional Dependency ($X \rightarrow Y$)**: States that attribute set X uniquely determines attribute set Y (e.g. `Student_ID -> Student_Name`).
topics.real_world_analogy: Storing customer details inside an orders table is like stapling a customer's full home address and credit history onto every single paper receipt. If the customer moves, you have to update thousands of old receipts (Update Anomaly). If they cancel an order, you throw away their only customer profile (Deletion Anomaly).
why_it_exists: Eliminate duplicate storage of repeated attribute values.
Guarantee data integrity across database modifications.
tech_world: OLTP relational databases (e.g. banking, billing) are normalized to 3NF/BCNF to prevent update anomalies under high write concurrency.
key_points: Insertion Anomaly: Inability to insert partial records.
Update Anomaly: Inconsistent updates across duplicate rows.
Deletion Anomaly: Unintended loss of unrelated data on deletion.
Functional Dependency (X -> Y): X uniquely identifies Y.
interview_focus: Explain the three database anomalies with examples.
How do Functional Dependencies determine database normal forms?

interview_questions.question: What is a Deletion Anomaly?
interview_questions.answer: A Deletion Anomaly occurs when deleting a row to remove one piece of data accidentally destroys unrelated critical data stored in the same row (e.g., deleting a student record also deletes the only record of a course).

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Bad Schema (Un-normalized):
Emp_ID | Emp_Name | Dept_ID | Dept_Name    | Dept_Head
101    | Alice    | D1      | Engineering  | Dr. Smith
102    | Bob      | D1      | Engineering  | Dr. Smith  <-- Duplicated!

Anomalies:
- Update: Changing Dept_Head requires updating N rows.
- Deletion: Deleting Alice & Bob wipes out Department D1 details!
quickRevisionNotes: Normalization eliminates Insertion, Update, and Deletion anomalies.
Functional Dependency X -> Y means X uniquely determines Y.

topics.title: Normal Forms Masterclass (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF) & Decomposition Tests
topics.what_is_it: Normal Forms are progressive criteria for database schema design: 1NF (Atomic Values), 2NF (No Partial Dependency), 3NF (No Transitive Dependency), and BCNF (Strict Determinant Candidate Key).
topics.simple_explanation:
Database schema normalization progresses through strict mathematical stages:

1. **First Normal Form (1NF)**: Every column cell must contain atomic (indivisible) single values. No repeating groups or arrays.
2. **Second Normal Form (2NF)**: Must be in 1NF AND have **No Partial Dependency**. Every non-prime attribute must depend on the FULL candidate key (not a partial subset of a composite candidate key).
3. **Third Normal Form (3NF)**: Must be in 2NF AND have **No Transitive Dependency**. Non-prime attributes must not depend on other non-prime attributes ($X \rightarrow Y$ where neither is a key).
4. **Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)**: Stricter version of 3NF. For EVERY functional dependency $X \rightarrow Y$, $X$ **MUST be a Super Key**.

**Decomposition Tests**:
- **Lossless Join Test**: Decomposing table $R$ into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless if $R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_1$ OR $R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_2$.
- **Dependency Preservation Test**: All original FDs must be enforce-able without joining decomposed tables.
topics.real_world_analogy: 1NF is like putting 1 item in 1 box (no bags of mixed items). 2NF is like ensuring an item tag depends on the whole box label, not half of it. 3NF is like eliminating middleman dependencies. BCNF is like ensuring only authorized primary key holders can decide attributes.
why_it_exists: Provide formal mathematical guarantees against structural redundancy.
Guide DBAs on decomposing monolithic tables safely without data loss.
tech_world: Most commercial production OLTP schemas are normalized to 3NF or BCNF.
key_points: 1NF: Atomic cell values.
2NF: 1NF + No Partial Dependency (Non-prime depends on full PK).
3NF: 2NF + No Transitive Dependency ($X \rightarrow Y$ non-prime to non-prime).
BCNF: For every $X \rightarrow Y$, $X$ MUST be a Super Key.
Lossless Join: $R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_1$ or $R_2$.
interview_focus: What is the difference between 3NF and BCNF?
How do you test if a table decomposition is Lossless or Lossy?

interview_questions.question: What is the key difference between 3NF and BCNF?
interview_questions.answer: In 3NF, for $X \rightarrow Y$, $X$ can be a Super Key OR $Y$ can be a Prime Attribute. In BCNF, there is no exception for $Y$: $X$ MUST strictly be a Super Key for every functional dependency.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Normal Form Progression:
1NF (Atomic Cells) 
  --> 2NF (Eliminate Partial Dependencies)
    --> 3NF (Eliminate Transitive Dependencies)
      --> BCNF (Every Determinant X is a Super Key)

Lossless Join Formula for R -> R1, R2:
(R1 ∩ R2 -> R1)  OR  (R1 ∩ R2 -> R2)
quickRevisionNotes: 2NF eliminates Partial Dependency; 3NF eliminates Transitive Dependency.
BCNF requires every determinant X in X -> Y to be a Super Key.

topics.title: Denormalization & Real-World System Performance Trade-offs
topics.what_is_it: Denormalization is the intentional optimization technique of adding redundant data or grouping tables back together to eliminate expensive joins in read-heavy analytical workloads.
topics.simple_explanation:
While 3NF/BCNF normalization is ideal for transactional OLTP writes, joining 10 normalized tables for complex analytical queries (OLAP) causes massive disk I/O and latency.

**Denormalization** intentionally introduces duplicate columns (e.g. copying `customer_name` directly into the `orders` table) or pre-aggregated summary tables. This speeds up read queries from $O(\text{JOIN})$ to $O(1)$, at the cost of slower writes and requiring application triggers to keep duplicate fields updated.
topics.real_world_analogy: Normalization is like storing bike parts in separate labeled boxes (Wheels, Chain, Frame) to keep inventory clean. If a customer buys a complete bike, assembling it on the spot (Joining) takes time. Denormalization is like pre-assembling complete bikes in the showroom so buyers can drive off immediately.
why_it_exists: Eliminate multi-table JOIN latency in read-heavy analytics dashboards.
Optimize Data Warehouses (Star Schema / Snowflake Schema) for fast aggregate reporting.
tech_world: Data Warehouses (Amazon Redshift, Snowflake, ClickHouse) intentionally use denormalized wide tables (Columnar Storage) for sub-second analytical reporting.
key_points: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing): Highly Normalized (3NF/BCNF) for fast, anomaly-free writes.
OLAP (Online Analytical Processing): Denormalized (Star Schema) for fast complex read aggregation.
Trade-off: Fast read queries vs Slower write updates and duplicate storage cost.
interview_focus: When should a database designer intentionally denormalize a database schema?
What are the trade-offs between OLTP normalized schemas and OLAP denormalized schemas?

interview_questions.question: What are the engineering trade-offs of denormalizing a database?
interview_questions.answer: Benefits: Faster read query performance by eliminating expensive multi-table JOINs. Costs: Increased storage overhead, slower write operations (INSERT/UPDATE), and the risk of data inconsistency if application triggers fail to update redundant duplicate columns.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Normalized (3NF):  Orders (id, cust_id) JOIN Customers (cust_id, name) -- Requires Join!
Denormalized:    Orders (id, cust_id, cust_name_copy)               -- 0 Joins!
quickRevisionNotes: Denormalization speeds up reads by trading off write speed and storage space.
OLTP uses normalized schemas; OLAP uses denormalized schemas.

topics.title: Transaction States & ACID Properties Mechanics
topics.what_is_it: A Transaction is a single logical unit of database work consisting of one or more SQL statements. ACID properties guarantee database validity despite crashes or concurrent access.
topics.simple_explanation:
Transactions enforce the 4 ACID guarantees:

1. **Atomicity ('All or Nothing')**: Every statement in a transaction executes successfully, or the entire transaction is completely aborted and rolled back using the Undo Log. No partial execution.
2. **Consistency**: Moves database from one valid state satisfying all schema constraints to another valid state.
3. **Isolation**: Concurrent transactions execute as if they were running sequentially in isolation, enforced via locks (2PL) or MVCC.
4. **Durability**: Once a transaction commits, its changes are permanently written to non-volatile disk storage (via WAL log sync) and survive power failures.

**5 Transaction Lifecycle States**:
Active -> Partially Committed -> Committed (Terminal State)
Active -> Failed -> Aborted (Terminal State).
topics.real_world_analogy: Transferring $100 from Account A to Account B requires 2 steps: Debit A, Credit B. Atomicity ensures if power fails after Debit A, $100 is returned to A. Durability ensures that once you see 'Transfer Successful', a power outage at the bank 1 second later won't erase the transfer.
why_it_exists: Protect financial transactions and critical business logic from system crashes.
Provide deterministic safe execution abstractions for multi-threaded server environments.
tech_world: Relational engines call `fsync()` on Write-Ahead Log (WAL) files during `COMMIT` to guarantee Durability before returning success to application clients.
key_points: Atomicity: Enforced via UNDO Logs.
Consistency: Enforced via schema constraints & application logic.
Isolation: Enforced via Concurrency Control (Locks / MVCC).
Durability: Enforced via REDO Logs & WAL `fsync()`.
States: Active -> Partially Committed -> Committed | Active -> Failed -> Aborted.
interview_focus: Explain how the database engine guarantees Atomicity during a crash.
What is the difference between Partially Committed and Committed transaction states?

interview_questions.question: What happens in the 'Partially Committed' state of a transaction?
interview_questions.answer: In the Partially Committed state, the final SQL statement has executed in RAM buffers, but log records have not yet been permanently flushed to disk via `fsync()`. If a crash occurs in this state, the transaction transitions to Failed and is Aborted.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Transaction Lifecycle State Diagram:
[ Active ] ---> [ Partially Committed ] ---> [ Committed ] (SUCCESS!)
    |                      |
    v                      v
 [ Failed ] -----------> [ Aborted ] (ROLLED BACK!)
quickRevisionNotes: ACID = Atomicity (Undo Log), Consistency, Isolation (Locks), Durability (WAL).
Committed means changes are permanently written to disk.

topics.title: Schedules, Conflict & View Serializability
topics.what_is_it: Serializability is the correctness criterion for concurrent transaction execution. A concurrent schedule is Conflict Serializable if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting operations.
topics.simple_explanation:
When transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ run concurrently, their read/write operations interleave in a **Schedule**. A schedule is safe if it is **Serializable** (produces identical results to running $T_1$ then $T_2$ sequentially).

**Conflict Operations**: Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, access the SAME data item, and at least ONE operation is a WRITE ($W(X)$):
1. $Read(X) - Write(X)$ (RAW conflict)
2. $Write(X) - Read(X)$ (WAR conflict)
3. $Write(X) - Write(X)$ (WAW conflict)

**Precedence Graph (Serialization Graph) Cycle Test**:
Create a graph where nodes are transactions. Draw a directed edge $T_i \rightarrow T_j$ if $T_i$ executes a conflicting operation BEFORE $T_j$.
- **If Graph has NO Cycle**: Schedule is **Conflict Serializable**! Topological sort gives equivalent Serial Order.
- **If Graph HAS a Cycle**: Schedule is NOT Conflict Serializable!
topics.real_world_analogy: Think of two chefs sharing one stove. If Chef 1 boils water and Chef 2 cuts vegetables (non-conflicting), order doesn't matter. If both try to adjust the temperature dial of the same burner (conflicting Write-Write), the execution order dictates whether the food burns!
why_it_exists: Mathematically prove whether a multi-threaded transaction schedule is safe from concurrency bugs.
tech_world: Database lock managers use precedence graphs or 2-Phase Locking to prevent cycle formation during concurrent transaction scheduling.
key_points: Conflicting Operations: Different transactions + Same data item + At least one Write.
Precedence Graph: Edge $T_i \rightarrow T_j$ for conflicting operation sequence.
No Cycle in Precedence Graph = Conflict Serializable!
Topological Sort = Equivalent Serial Order.
interview_focus: How do you test if a concurrent transaction schedule is Conflict Serializable?
What are the 3 types of operation conflicts in transaction processing?

interview_questions.question: How do you detect if a concurrent schedule of 3 transactions is Conflict Serializable?
interview_questions.answer: Construct a Precedence Graph with nodes $T_1, T_2, T_3$. Draw directed edges $T_i \rightarrow T_j$ for every pair of conflicting operations where $T_i$ executed first. Run Kahn's Cycle Detection Algorithm. If no cycles exist, the schedule is Conflict Serializable; a topological sort yields the equivalent serial execution sequence.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Precedence Graph Cycle Test:
Schedule: R1(X), W2(X), W1(X)
- R1(X) -> W2(X)  gives edge T1 -> T2
- W2(X) -> W1(X)  gives edge T2 -> T1
Graph: T1 <---> T2  (CYCLE DETECTED! NOT Conflict Serializable!)
quickRevisionNotes: No cycle in Precedence Graph = Conflict Serializable.
Conflicts occur when 2 transactions access the same item and at least 1 is a Write.

topics.title: Schedule Recoverability: Recoverable, Cascadeless & Strict Schedules
topics.what_is_it: Schedule Recoverability ensures that if a transaction aborts, the database can recover without cascading rollbacks or dirty read corruptions.
topics.simple_explanation:
Even if a schedule is serializable, it might be unrecoverable if a transaction reads uncommitted data:

1. **Recoverable Schedule**: If $T_2$ reads data written by $T_1$, then $T_1$ MUST commit BEFORE $T_2$ commits. (Prevents dirty commit failures).
2. **Cascadeless Schedule**: $T_2$ is NOT ALLOWED to read data written by $T_1$ until $T_1$ has committed! (Prevents **Cascading Aborts** where aborting $T_1$ forces 100 dependent transactions to abort).
3. **Strict Schedule**: $T_2$ is NOT ALLOWED to READ OR WRITE data written by $T_1$ until $T_1$ commits/aborts. (Allows super-easy recovery using simple undo logs!).
topics.real_world_analogy: Cascading abort is like a rumor in a company. Employee 1 tells unverified rumor (uncommitted write) to Employee 2, who tells 50 others. When Employee 1 retracts the rumor (aborts), management has to spend hours tracking down and correcting all 50 employees (Cascading Abort!). A Cascadeless schedule prohibits sharing rumors until management officially confirms them.
why_it_exists: Prevent disastrous cascading rollbacks where 1 aborting transaction forces cancellation of thousands of concurrent operations.
Simplify database crash recovery algorithms.
tech_world: Modern commercial database lock managers enforce **Strict 2PL**, which guarantees Strict Schedules and complete immunity to cascading aborts.
key_points: Recoverable: $T_1$ commits before $T_2$ commits (if $T_2$ reads $T_1$'s write).
Cascadeless: $T_2$ cannot READ $T_1$'s uncommitted write.
Strict: $T_2$ cannot READ or WRITE $T_1$'s uncommitted data.
Hierarchy: Strict ⊂ Cascadeless ⊂ Recoverable.
interview_focus: What is a Cascading Abort and how do Cascadeless schedules prevent it?
What is the hierarchy between Recoverable, Cascadeless, and Strict schedules?

interview_questions.question: What is a Strict Schedule and why do commercial databases enforce it?
interview_questions.answer: A Strict Schedule requires that uncommitted data modified by $T_1$ cannot be read OR overwritten by any other transaction until $T_1$ commits or aborts. Commercial databases enforce Strict 2PL to guarantee Strict Schedules because abort recovery simply requires restoring pre-transaction values from the undo log without checking other transactions.

topics.syntaxOrCode:
Hierarchy of Schedules:
[ All Concurrent Schedules ]
   └── [ Recoverable Schedules ]
          └── [ Cascadeless Schedules ]
                 └── [ Strict Schedules ] (Enforced by Strict 2PL!)
quickRevisionNotes: Cascadeless schedules prohibit reading uncommitted writes.
Strict 2PL guarantees Strict Schedules and prevents cascading rollbacks.
